lesson.title: The Hidden Logic Behind Bad Decisions
lesson.summary: This section introduces cognitive bias as predictable, systematic errors in thinking that shape both the choices historical actors made and the conclusions historians draw about causation.
lesson.body:
You already know that explaining historical causation means identifying the chain of conditions and choices that produced an outcome. But to explain *why* people made the choices they did, you often need something more than "they had reasons" ,  you need to understand that human reasoning itself follows predictable patterns, and some of those patterns systematically pull people away from the most rational choice available. Psychologists call these patterns cognitive biases. They are not random mistakes or signs of stupidity; they are consistent, repeatable distortions that show up across different people, cultures, and time periods, which is exactly what makes them useful tools for historical analysis.

The underlying mechanism is that the human brain rarely has time to weigh every piece of evidence before acting, so it relies on mental shortcuts that usually work well enough. The problem is that these shortcuts fail in specific, predictable ways under specific conditions, and those failure patterns are what we call biases. Take the sunk cost fallacy: rational decision-making says you should only weigh future costs and benefits, since past investment can't be recovered no matter what you choose next. But people consistently keep pouring resources into a failing course of action specifically because they've already invested heavily in it, as if quitting would somehow erase the earlier loss. A military commander who keeps sending troops into a costly offensive partly because so many lives and resources have already been spent on it is a textbook case ,  the past investment is psychologically pulling on a decision that should only be about the future.

Confirmation bias works through a different mechanism: once someone holds a belief, they pay closer attention to evidence that supports it and discount or reinterpret evidence that contradicts it. This isn't necessarily dishonest; it happens because confirming evidence feels easier to process and fits an existing mental picture, while disconfirming evidence creates uncomfortable tension that the mind is motivated to resolve by dismissing it. A policymaker convinced that a strategy is working will tend to notice reports that support that conclusion and explain away reports that don't, which means the strategy can keep going long after the evidence against it has piled up.

Groupthink adds a social layer to the same problem: when a group of decision-makers values consensus and loyalty highly, individual members become reluctant to voice doubts, fearing they'll disrupt group harmony or be seen as disloyal. The mechanism here is social pressure suppressing critical evaluation, so a room full of capable people can collectively reach a worse decision than any one of them might have reached alone, simply because dissent gets filtered out before it can influence the discussion.

These biases matter to you as a student of causation in two directions. First, they help explain otherwise puzzling historical decisions ,  why leaders escalated a failing policy, like the continued buildup of U.S. involvement in Vietnam despite growing evidence the approach wasn't achieving its goals, becomes more understandable once you factor in sunk costs, selective attention to favorable reports, and pressure toward consensus among advisers. Second, and just as important, historians themselves are vulnerable to bias, especially hindsight bias ,  the tendency to see an outcome as having been more predictable or inevitable than it actually was once you already know how events turned out. Recognizing that risk is part of building a causal explanation you can actually trust.
